title: Effective AI rollout depends on rare implementers combining procedural, technical and political knowledge—and peer diffusion over training modules
text: Card 9 places the real AI implementer at the rare intersection of three kinds of knowledge rarely held in one head: procedural (how the work really runs), technological (what the tech really does) and political (who will block it). Against a Microsoft and LinkedIn Work Trend Index 2024 baseline where 75 of 100 knowledge workers use AI at work (59 with their own tools) while 60% of leaders report no implementation plan, Messy Jobs highlights three practices shared by the strongest implementers: speed (deploy before resistance forms), scarcity and status (make access scarce so it becomes a status symbol) and autonomy (let peers teach peers instead of formal training modules).
qualification: Conceptual Venn model and practitioner synthesis from Card 9 (citing Messy Jobs pp. 100–115 and Microsoft/LinkedIn Work Trend Index 2024, N=31,000); the three implementation tactics (speed, artificial scarcity and peer autonomy) carry governance risks if applied without data-security or risk controls.
